followUps:
Stop, say it out loud, and decide whether to patch or restructure. The quickest way is to name the flaw calmly: "this state shape makes cancel hard, so I will change it before adding more." Interviewers like seeing you notice early more than they dislike a change.

Check what you can keep: usually helpers and tests survive, only the core data structure changes. Example: if you stored results with push and need input order, switch to results[i] and keep the rest. Spend at most 5 minutes on a rewrite; if it is more, tell them the trade-off and finish the simpler version first.

Roughly 15 to 20 percent of the time, spread through the session rather than all at the end. That is about 10 to 15 minutes in a 75 minute round.

Run one tiny case right after the happy path works (about 2 minutes), then test each edge case as you add it (empty input, error, repeated call). Keep the last 5 minutes for one failure case and a short summary of what you would add next. Tests with real numbers, like debounce with events at 0, 30, 60, show correctness better than silence.

code.title: myCall polyfill with Symbol key and finally cleanup

followUps:
Build apply by spreading the array into your call: the array becomes the argument list.

Function.prototype.myApply = function (ctx, arr) {
  return this.myCall(ctx, ...(arr || []));
};
// greet.myApply(user, ['Hi', '!']) -> same as myCall(user, 'Hi', '!')

Handle arr being null or undefined (native allows that and passes no args). Native apply also accepts array-likes such as arguments; use Array.from(arr) if you want that.

Because the function might throw, and without finally the temporary Symbol property would stay on the object forever.

Example: boom.myCall(user) throws. With plain code after the call, delete ctx[key] is skipped and user now carries a hidden property (we saw 1 key instead of 0). finally runs on both return and throw, so the object is always restored. Cost is nothing extra.

Use a string key made unlikely to clash, and arguments plus eval-free argument passing through apply, which already exists in ES5.

Function.prototype.myCall = function (ctx) {
  ctx = ctx == null ? window : Object(ctx);
  var key = '__fn' + Date.now() + Math.random();
  ctx[key] = this;
  var args = Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments, 1);
  try { return ctx[key].apply(ctx, args); }
  finally { delete ctx[key]; }
};

Risk: the string key could in theory collide or show in for...in during the call.

code.title: Promise.all polyfill: order, empty input, first rejection

followUps:
allSettled never rejects and reports every outcome; any resolves with the first success and rejects only if all fail.

// allSettled: store {status, value|reason} at index i, resolve at remaining === 0
items.forEach((it, i) => Promise.resolve(it).then(
  v => { out[i] = {status:'fulfilled', value:v}; done(); },
  r => { out[i] = {status:'rejected', reason:r}; done(); }));
// any: resolve on first success, count errors, reject when errors === n

For any, reject with an AggregateError holding the errors in order. Empty input: allSettled resolves [], any rejects at once.

Do not start everything at once: keep a cursor and run at most N tasks at a time (a pool of workers).

Each worker loops: take the next index, await the task, store results[i], repeat until the cursor reaches the end. With 10 tasks and limit 3, only 3 run together and the result order still matches input order. Because promises start work when created, the input must be functions (() => fetch(url)), not already-started promises. Time is about total work divided by N.

The first rejection wins, and the other promises are not cancelled; they keep running and their results are simply ignored.

If another one also rejects later, it is still handled, because then(..., reject) attached a handler to every promise, so there is no unhandled rejection warning. Calling reject twice is harmless since a promise settles once. If you had not attached handlers to all items, Node would report unhandled rejections. To really stop work, pass an AbortController signal.

code.title: Debounce vs throttle timeline on a fake clock

followUps:
Debounce with maxWait is a debounce that is forced to fire if events keep arriving too long, which gives a throttle-like guarantee.

function throttle(fn, wait) {
  return debounce(fn, wait, { maxWait: wait });
}
// inside debounce: on each call, fire when quiet for wait
// OR when now - firstCallTime >= maxWait

With wait 100 and events every 30 ms, plain debounce never fires, while maxWait 100 fires roughly at 0..100, 100..200 and so on. This is how lodash builds throttle.

Replace the clock and timers with fakes, so the test jumps forward in time instantly.

Jest has jest.useFakeTimers() and advanceTimersByTime(100); Node has mock.timers. As in the program, you can also inject setTimeout yourself. Test: call at 0, 30, 60, advance 99 (not called), advance 1 more (called once with the last args). Test with a leading option, cancel and flush too. Tests run in milliseconds and are never flaky.

Each render creates a brand new debounced function with its own timer, so the debouncing silently stops working.

If typing triggers a state change and a re-render, the next keystroke calls a different debounced function than the one holding the pending timer. Result: every keystroke fires, just delayed. Fix: create it once with useMemo or useRef (and keep the latest callback in a ref), and cancel it in the effect cleanup on unmount.

code.title: Deep clone with WeakMap: cycles, shared refs, prototypes

followUps:
Use an explicit stack instead of recursion, so very deep objects do not overflow the call stack.

const seen = new WeakMap(), root = {};
const stack = [[src, root]];
seen.set(src, root);
while (stack.length) {
  const [from, to] = stack.pop();
  for (const k of Reflect.ownKeys(from)) { /* if object: make copy, seen.set, push pair */ }
}

The copy is created first and filled later, so cycles still work. Recursion depth is about 10,000 frames in V8; the stack version only uses heap memory.

A function's behaviour depends on its closure (the variables around where it was created), and that cannot be copied across the structured clone format.

The algorithm serialises data, not code or scope, so structuredClone({f(){}}) throws DataCloneError. Same for DOM nodes and Symbols. If you need to copy a function reference, copy it by reference (the same function object is shared) in a custom clone, which is safe because functions are usually immutable.

They copy only the parts that changed along the path, and share everything else by reference.

Example: state {a:{x:1}, b:{y:2}}, update a.x to 5: {...s, a:{...s.a, x:5}} makes 2 new objects, while b is reused. Cost is proportional to the depth of the change, not the size of the state. Reused references also let React skip work with a cheap === check. Libraries such as Immer automate this.

code.title: deepEqual: NaN, Dates, Sets, key order, cycles

followUps:
Because deep comparison costs time proportional to the whole data, and React must check props on every render.

Shallow compare checks each top-level key with Object.is: O(k) for k keys. It works because React state is treated as immutable: a changed object always gets a new reference, so an unchanged reference means "nothing changed inside". Deep equality on a 10,000-item list each render would be far slower and still wrong for functions.

Return a list of changes with a path to each, instead of stopping at the first difference.

function diff(a, b, path = '', out = []) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) return out;
  if (isObj(a) && isObj(b))
    for (const k of new Set([...Object.keys(a), ...Object.keys(b)]))
      diff(a[k], b[k], path + '/' + k, out);
  else out.push({ path, from: a, to: b });
  return out;
}

Example: {a:1,b:2} vs {a:1,b:3} gives [{path:'/b', from:2, to:3}]. Arrays and cycles need the same care as in deepEqual.

code.title: curry: collecting arguments until fn.length

followUps:
Pick a unique placeholder value, and when merging new arguments, fill the placeholder slots first.

const _ = Symbol('hole');
function merge(prev, next) {
  const out = prev.map(a => (a === _ && next.length ? next.shift() : a));
  return out.concat(next);
}
// ready when out.length >= fn.length and no _ remains

Example: c(_, 2)(1) with a 3-argument function: first [_, 2], then 1 fills the hole to give [1, 2], still waiting for the third.

sum(1)(2)(3)() works because each call returns a function until an empty call asks for the total; the valueOf trick lets the function itself act like a number.

function sum(a) {
  const f = b => sum(a + b);
  f.valueOf = () => a;   // used when coerced: +sum(1)(2)(3) === 6
  return f;
}

Using f in arithmetic or template strings triggers coercion, which calls valueOf. It is a party trick: it returns a function, not a number, so === comparisons fail.

code.title: EventEmitter: snapshot emit, once, safe off

followUps:
Make emit await each listener's result and return when they all finish.

async emit(name, ...args) {
  const list = [...(this.map.get(name) || [])];
  await Promise.all(list.map(l => l(...args)));  // parallel
  return list.length > 0;
}

Decide: parallel (Promise.all, one failure rejects) or serial (for...of with await, ordered but slower). With 3 listeners of 10 ms each, parallel takes about 10 ms and serial about 30 ms.

Store wildcard patterns in a separate list and also call them on every emit.

Example: on('user.*', fn). On emit('user.login'), call the exact listeners, then each pattern whose regex matches (convert * to [^.]+). Pass the event name as an extra first argument so a wildcard handler knows what fired. Cost: emit becomes O(number of patterns), so keep patterns few or index by prefix.

EventTarget uses event objects and the DOM's rules, while a typical emitter passes plain arguments.

Differences: listeners receive one Event object (data in event.detail for CustomEvent); it supports {once, signal} options, capture/bubble phases, and preventDefault; duplicate registration of the same function and options is ignored, whereas Node's emitter adds it twice; and a throwing listener does not stop others (the error is reported).

code.title: retry with backoff, full jitter and injectable sleep

followUps:
Jitter spreads the retries of many clients over time, so they do not all hit the struggling server at the same instant.

Without jitter, 1,000 clients that failed together all retry at 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms: waves of 1,000 requests. With full jitter each waits a random time up to the cap, so the 1,000 retries spread across the window, about 10 per millisecond for a 100 ms cap. The server recovers instead of being knocked down again.

Retry amplification is when each layer retries, so one failure turns into a huge number of requests.

Example: 3 layers each try 3 times, so the bottom service sees 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls for one user action, right when it is already overloaded. Prevent it by retrying at one layer only, using a retry budget (for example at most 10 percent extra traffic), and circuit breakers that stop calls to a dead dependency.

Mostly the same way as any HTTP client: they retry some errors with backoff and honour the server's wait hint.

On a 429 (rate limit) the response often includes a retry-after header, which says how many seconds to wait. Typical SDK behaviour is a small number of retries (2 or so) with exponential backoff and jitter, also for 5xx and connection errors, and a configurable max. Check your SDK's docs for exact defaults. In your own code, also cap total time and avoid retrying non-idempotent calls blindly.

code.title: LRU cache with Map insertion order

followUps:
Store an expiry time with each value and treat expired entries as missing.

put(k, v, ttl) { this.m.delete(k); this.m.set(k, { v, exp: Date.now() + ttl }); /* evict LRU */ }
get(k) {
  const e = this.m.get(k);
  if (!e) return undefined;
  if (e.exp <= Date.now()) { this.m.delete(k); return undefined; }  // lazy expiry
  this.m.delete(k); this.m.set(k, e); return e.v;
}

Lazy expiry is O(1); add a periodic sweep so expired entries that are never read do not stay in memory.

Keep a map from key to node, and a map from use-count to a linked list of keys with that count, plus a minCount pointer.

On get, move the key from list c to list c+1; if list minCount is now empty, raise minCount. On put of a new key when full, evict the oldest key in list minCount, then set minCount = 1. Every step touches a few pointers, so each operation is O(1). Ties between equal counts are broken by LRU order.

Redis does not track exact order; it samples a few random keys and evicts the oldest among them.

With maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, Redis picks maxmemory-samples keys (default 5) and removes the one idle longest. This saves the memory and time of a full linked list. A larger sample (10) is closer to true LRU. The trade-off is small inaccuracy for much lower overhead.

code.title: Event loop order: sync, nextTick, microtasks, timers

followUps:
It would appear last, after 1 4 2 3, because a timer callback is a macrotask.

Order with the timer added: 1 4 2 3 5. All microtasks (2 and 3) drain before the event loop picks the next macrotask, even when the timer delay is 0. Delay 0 only means "as soon as possible after the current work", never "before microtasks".

Older engines (before 2018-2019) took extra ticks to resolve await, so the order of 2 and 3 could differ.

Early implementations wrapped the awaited value in extra promises, costing about 3 microtask ticks. A spec change (V8 7.2 / Node 12) made await of a native promise or plain value take just 1 tick. That is why an old article may show 3 before 2 and modern Node prints 2 before 3.

It schedules a function to run as a microtask, without creating a promise.

queueMicrotask(() => console.log('micro'));
console.log('sync');
// prints: sync, then micro

It runs after the current synchronous code but before any timer or I/O. Use it to defer work slightly while keeping it before rendering. An endless chain of microtasks starves the event loop, so the page or process never reaches timers.

code.title: Why [] == ![] is true, and strict vs loose equality
code.js:
// Coercion: why [] == ![] is true, step by step
console.log('![]            :', ![]);                // object is truthy -> false
console.log('Number(false)  :', Number(false));      // boolean -> number 0
console.log('String([])     :', JSON.stringify(String([])));  // toString -> ""
console.log('Number("")     :', Number(''));         // "" -> 0
console.log('[] == ![]      :', [] == ![]);          // 0 == 0
console.log('[] === ![]     :', [] === ![]);         // strict: no coercion

console.log('null >= 0      :', null >= 0);          // relational: null -> 0
console.log('null == 0      :', null == 0);          // == special: null only equals undefined
console.log('null == undef  :', null == undefined);

console.log('isNaN("abc")   :', isNaN('abc'));       // coerces first
console.log('Number.isNaN   :', Number.isNaN('abc'));// no coercion
console.log('"5" + 1, "5"-1 :', '5' + 1, '5' - 1);
const x = undefined;
console.log('x == null idiom:', x == null);          // null or undefined only

followUps:
ToPrimitive is the internal step that turns an object into a primitive value (string or number) so it can be compared or added.

It calls valueOf() first, and if that still returns an object, toString() (the order flips for hint "string", and Symbol.toPrimitive wins if defined). For [], valueOf returns the array itself, so toString() gives "". For [1,2] it gives "1,2". That is why [1,2] + 1 is "1,21".

Because >= converts null to the number 0, but == has a special rule that null only equals undefined.

So null >= 0 becomes 0 >= 0, true. null > 0 is false and null <= 0 is true, which is why the odd result shows up. The rule for == never converts null or undefined to numbers, so null == 0 is false. Use === and explicit checks to avoid this.

code.title: Promise pool: limited concurrency, ordered results

followUps:
Here is the pool in short form: workers share a cursor and write results by index.

async function pool(tasks, n) {
  const out = [];
  let i = 0;
  const worker = async () => {
    while (i < tasks.length) { const k = i++; out[k] = await tasks[k](); }
  };
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: n }, worker));
  return out;
}

i++ is safe because JavaScript is single-threaded: no two workers can claim the same index. Add try/catch inside for allSettled-style results.

Start from the API's documented limits, then measure, and adjust until throughput stops improving or errors appear.

Example: if the API allows 50 requests per second and each call takes about 200 ms, concurrency 10 gives 10 / 0.2 = 50 requests per second. Higher only adds 429s. Also consider your own sockets and memory. Start with 10, double while latency stays flat, back off when you see 429 or timeouts (adaptive concurrency).

Save progress as you go, then on restart skip what was already done.

After each success, record the task id (a file, database row or a checkpoint of the last contiguous index). On restart load the done set and run only the rest. Make each call idempotent or use an idempotency key, because a task that finished on the server but was not recorded will run twice. Batching checkpoints (every 100 tasks) reduces write cost but repeats up to 100 tasks after a crash.

A classic one is a debounce that loses this or the latest arguments, for example using an arrow wrapper or storing only the first call's arguments.

// buggy: arguments from the FIRST call are used
function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let t;
  return (...a) => { if (!t) t = setTimeout(() => fn(...a), ms); };
}

It never resets the timer, so it is not a debounce at all (it fires ms after the first event with the first args). The fix is to clearTimeout(t) on every call and use the newest arguments. Another common one: it forgets to clear the timer on cancel.

Write quick property tests and a few edge cases, and compare them with a simple trusted model.

Test: capacity 2, put a, put b, get a, put c: b must be evicted, not a. Also check updating an existing key does not grow size, capacity 1, and get on a missing key. Run a random sequence of 10,000 operations against a naive array-based LRU and compare results after each step. It takes minutes, and catches most recency bugs.

code.title: Leaks: listeners with and without AbortController, bounded cache

followUps:
WeakMap holds an object key weakly and is for data attached to an object; WeakRef holds a value weakly and is for caching things you can rebuild.

Use WeakMap when the key object's lifetime should control the entry (metadata for a DOM node). Use WeakRef plus a FinalizationRegistry to cache large results by a string key, and then the map itself still needs to remove dead keys. Garbage collection timing is not guaranteed, so never rely on it for logic, only for saving memory.

Take two heap snapshots around the action and look for "Detached" nodes in the comparison, then follow the retainers.

In Chrome DevTools Memory: take a snapshot, open and close the view (for example a modal, 5 times), take another, and filter by "Detached". Select a detached element and read the Retainers panel: it shows the chain, such as window.handler -> closure -> element. Typical causes are listeners not removed, timers still running, or a global array holding the node.
